1. Introduction & Clinical Context
The investigation of hepatobiliary disorders requires a logical, stepwise approach combining clinical
presentation with laboratory, radiological, and histopathological evaluations. In clinical practice, liver diseases
usually manifest as acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, cholestasis (obstructive or hepatocellular), or
incidental abnormalities discovered on routine screening. Investigations are systematically designed to
determine the presence of liver disease, classify the type of injury (hepatocellular vs. cholestatic), evaluate
synthetic function, and identify the specific etiology. 
2. Laboratory Investigations: Liver Function Tests (LFTs)
Standard "Liver Function Tests" is a broad term that includes enzymes reflecting hepatocyte integrity or biliary
clearance, as well as true markers of hepatic synthetic capacity. 
A. Markers of Hepatocellular Injury (Aminotransferases)
Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT): Primarily localized to the liver cytosol; highly specific for hepatic
parenchymal injury.
Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST): Present in liver (cytosol and mitochondria), cardiac muscle, skeletal
muscle, kidneys, and brain. Less specific than ALT.
Clinical Interpretation of Aminotransferase Elevations:
Marked elevation (>1000 U/L): Suggests acute ischemic injury (shock liver), acute viral hepatitis, or toxin/
drug-induced liver injury (e.g., acetaminophen toxicity).
Mild-to-moderate elevation (<300 U/L): Common in Chronic Hepatitis B/C, Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver
Disease (NAFLD/MASLD), and Alcoholic Liver Disease.
AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis Ratio): An AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 is highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease,
driven by pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency in alcoholics which selectively suppresses ALT. A ratio > 1 in
chronic viral hepatitis suggests progression to cirrhosis.
B. Markers of Cholestasis and Biliary Secretory Function
Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP): Synthesized by canalicular membranes of hepatocytes and bone, placenta,
and intestine. To confirm hepatic origin, pair it with Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) or fractionate
isoenzymes. Isolated high ALP with normal GGT points to bone pathology.
Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT): Highly sensitive for hepatobiliary disease but lacks specificity
(induced by alcohol ingestion, phenytoin, and various microsomal-inducing drugs).

C. True Markers of Hepatic Synthetic Capacity
Serum Albumin: Synthesized exclusively by the liver. Because it has a long half-life (~20 days), low serum
albumin is characteristic of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis) or severe protein-losing states, rather than
acute liver injury.
Prothrombin Time (PT) and INR: Measures the extrinsic clotting pathway dependent on factors I, II, V, VII,
and X. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (~6 hours), making PT/INR an excellent, highly sensitive indicator
of acute hepatic synthetic failure (e.g., fulminant hepatic failure) as well as chronic dysfunction.
D. Excretory Markers: Serum Bilirubin
Unconjugated (Indirect) Bilirubinemia: Driven by overproduction (hemolysis) or impaired hepatic
conjugation (e.g., Gilbert’s syndrome).
Conjugated (Direct) Bilirubinemia: Indicates parenchymal liver damage or biliary tree obstruction
(cholestasis). Direct bilirubin fraction > 50% confirms a conjugated pattern.

4th Year Exam Note: Vitamin K vs. Parenchymal Dysfunction
To differentiate prolonged PT caused by prolonged biliary obstruction (impaired fat-soluble Vitamin K absorption
due to lack of bile salts) from severe parenchymal failure, administer parenteral Vitamin K. If PT normalizes or
improves by >30% within 24–48 hours, the defect is obstructive/absorptive. If it fails to correct, it indicates
severe parenchymal synthetic failure. 
3. Etiological Investigations
Once a pattern of liver injury is established, specific serological, immunological, and metabolic profiles are
requested to ascertain the underlying etiology.

B. Autoimmune Liver Diseases
Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH): Characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG) and positive
autoantibodies: 
Type 1 AIH: Anti-Nuclear Antibody (ANA) and/or Anti-Smooth Muscle Antibody (ASMA).
Type 2 AIH: Anti-Liver Kidney Microsome type 1 (Anti-LKM-1) antibodies; typically seen in pediatric
populations.
Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC): Chronic cholestatic disease destroying intrahepatic small bile ducts.
Screening marker of choice is Anti-Mitochondrial Antibody (AMA), highly sensitive and specific (>95%).
Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC): Fibrosing inflammation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts,
strongly linked to Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD/Ulcerative Colitis). Associated with Perinuclear Anti-
Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (p-ANCA), though diagnosis depends primarily on imaging.
C. Metabolic and Genetic Inquiries
Hereditary Hemochromatosis: Screen via Transferrin Saturation (elevated, often >45-50%) and Serum
Ferritin. Confirmed via HFE gene mutation analysis (C282Y/H63D).
Wilson's Disease: Disorder of copper excretion, presenting with neuropsychiatric symptoms and liver
disease in young patients. Screen via reduced Serum Ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL) and elevated 24-hour
Urinary Copper Excretion. Slit-lamp exam reveals Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings.
Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (A1AT) Deficiency: Suspected in patients presenting with concomitant early-onset
emphysema and liver cirrhosis. Investigated via serum A1AT levels and Pi-phenotyping.
4. Imaging Modalities
A. Transabdominal Ultrasonography (US)
The indispensable first-line, non-invasive imaging modality for nearly all suspected liver diseases. 
Evaluates liver size, echogenicity (e.g., diffusely increased echogenicity indicating "fatty liver" / steatosis),
and surface contour (nodularity suggests cirrhosis).
Detects dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts to differentiate intrahepatic cholestasis from
mechanical extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
Evaluates for ascites, splenomegaly, and portal vein patency/flow direction using Doppler imaging.

B. Computed Tomography (CT) & Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Contrast-Enhanced Multi-phase CT/MRI: Critical for characterizing focal liver lesions (e.g., Hemangioma,
Adenoma, Focal Nodular Hyperplasia, and Hepatocellular Carcinoma [HCC]). HCC demonstrates a classic
dynamic pattern: arterial phase hyperenhancement followed by venous/delayed phase washout.
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP): Non-invasive T2-weighted MRI protocol
optimal for visualizing biliary tree anatomy. It is the gold standard for diagnosing PSC, showing a classic
"beaded appearance" of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
C. Non-Invasive Fibrosis Assessment: Transient Elastography (FibroScan)
Measures liver stiffness by calculating the velocity of a low-frequency shear wave passing through the
parenchyma. It has largely replaced diagnostic liver biopsies for staging fibrosis in chronic hepatitis B and C
and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). 
5. Endoscopic and Invasive Investigations
A. Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy - EGD)
Essential screening tool in patients diagnosed with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. It aims to identify, grade,
and prophylactically manage esophageal and gastric varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy to prevent
catastrophic variceal hemorrhage. 
B. Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
An invasive endoscopic-radiological tool. Due to procedural risks (e.g., post-ERCP pancreatitis, cholangitis), its
role has evolved to be primarily therapeutic rather than purely diagnostic. It is utilized for common bile duct
stone extraction, sphincterotomy, and biliary stenting across malignant or benign strictures. 
C. Histopathological Investigation: Liver Biopsy
Historically the absolute gold standard; currently reserved for cases where non-invasive testing yields
ambiguous or conflicting results. 
Indications: Staging and grading chronic viral hepatitis when non-invasive tools are unavailable; diagnosing
seronegative autoimmune hepatitis; evaluating unexplained hepatomegaly or persistent abnormal LFTs.
Absolute Contraindications: Severe uncorrectable coagulopathy (INR > 1.5), profound thrombocytopenia
(Platelets < 50,000/µL), suspected vascular tumors or echinococcal (hydatid) cysts, and uncooperative
patients.
6. Diagnostic Algorithm: Summary Framework
Step 1: Identify clinical syndrome (Acute liver failure, Jaundice, or Incidental abnormal LFTs).
Step 2: Evaluate standard LFTs. Categorize into Hepatocellular (ALT/AST dominant) or Cholestatic (ALP/
GGT dominant). Confirm synthetic reserve using PT/INR and Albumin.
Step 3: Order first-line Abdominal Ultrasound alongside initial baseline serologies (Viral markers for
hepatocellular; biliary evaluation for cholestasis).
Step 4: Advance to specific autoantibodies, metabolic screens, or specialized dynamic cross-sectional
imaging (MRCP/CT) based on Step 2 and 3 results.
